title: Marcelo Bielsa Tactics Explained
content: if your soul experience that Marcelo Bielsa was watching Leal's through yielder feet to Strasbourg in the second game of Liga this season you'd be forgiven for thinking he was something of a newcomer to football management there were three substitutions before half-time which forced Bielsa to play an outfielder in goal one smoke main and was sent off the outfielder was then swapped for another outfielder and the match descended into something of a farce but Marcelo Bielsa is in fact one of the most exciting innovative coaches in world football and his brand of attacking possession based football played with a high tempo and often based on a three three one three formation has influenced managers like Pep Guardiola Mauricio Pasha Tina and Diego Simeone Bielsa nicknamed el loco the mad one is obsessive in his preparation using videos to explain opposition systems to his teams he favors a three three one three formation which sees three central defenders a deep screening midfielder wide midfielders or wing backs a creative midfielder in the hole and a front three with two white men who stretched the play bielsa alters his formations to suit his opposition though sometimes using a 4-2-3-1 with high fall backs his aim is to have one more Center back than the opposition have strikers which facilitates his high line and pressing style of play as only one spare defender means there are more players to push forwards be also gets his teams to play with ferocious pace despite also favoring a possession based game this requires huge technical skill from his squad and he frequently plays midfielders such as Gary Modell or Leal's ibrahim al madhu in central defensive roles to ensure they have the ball skills to pass out from the back bielsa also uses full backs as centre backs because he believes they are better able to carry the ball and even deployed utter over dow as a wingback when coaching Chile his defenders are expected to pass the ball among themselves and the goalkeeper before recycling possession wide the essential shape of a bielsa three three one three which is his favorite system creates a kind of bowl shape in the defensive line with the deep midfielder dropping into that space to patrol the middle of the pitch and assisting the center box at Lille Thiago Mendez or Thiago Maia perform this role and they are the fulcrum around which much of the play rotates the wing backs or wide midfielders and with bielsa the distinction is blurred push high and often ahead of the holding midfielder ahead of them are the 1:3 component the element with which Bayelsa rarely if ever tinker's and were al-ghazi and Luis Serra at Lille play as wide as possible stretching the opponent's full backs and creating overloads in the wide spaces with the wing backs between them plays a striker Nikola deprave oh and what Argentinian football refers to as an encounter a literally a hook a playmaker with very limited defensive responsibilities who acts as a prompt for the attacking moves Yassine Ben Xia the former Leone player fulfills this role at Lille having been converted from a center for even one Bielsa abandoned the 331 3 Athletic Bilbao in favor of a four-man defence he played two holding midfielders behind an advanced and Gantt che and three forwards too wide the intention is to play with pace and width high up the pitch passing in triangles and moving off the ball to form a kind of attacking whirlwind the opposition players struggle to mark there is an emphasis on verticality transitioning the ball rapidly forwards to force the opposition back players rotate switching the focus of attack and are expected to be able to fill in for one another to improvise within the system there is something of the positional fluidity of Total Football in be else's approach he also preaches pressing Bielsa doesn't set up a team to play in a defensive block and an attacking one all of his players are expected to run and hassle while also playing a high line that minimizes the opposition's room to develop play the demands on PLC's players are as intense as his style of management and his style of football the physical demands are obvious but the mental ones are there to pre-plan passing moves must be learned the opposition studied to a meticulous degree and positional play mastered especially tricky when playing such an idiosyncratic formation but Marcelo Bielsa is without doubt something of a footballing genius and his tactics fluid erudite innovative demand more analysis than a short video like this can title: Inter Milan's 2009/10 Treble Tactics Explained
content: In the 200910 season, Jose Mourinho guided Inter Milan to an unprecedented treble. No Italian club has since won Syria, their domestic cup, the Copper Italia, and the UEFA Champions League in one season, and only six teams have done it ever. Inter are the most recent Italian team to win the Champions League and have not won a league title since the treble. While Mourinho has been categorized as a defensive coach, his 20089 title winning interside led the league in goals scored with 70 joint with AC Milan. While in 200910 they scored 75 goals, seven more than next best Roma. In both seasons, Mourinho's side also conceded the fewest. This partly stems from the Portuguese manager's superb defensive organization and his team's willingness to play almost exclusively on the counter. Mourinho set his side up as either a 4-312 or a 4231. Both systems were built on the rocksolid center back pairing of Lucio and Walter Samuel with Julio Cesar an adept reader of the game as a sweeper keeper operating behind. The defense sat deep and relied on the mobility of the midfield to cover. Club captain and legend Javier Zeneti played mostly at left back, though he was sometimes used in central midfield. Indeed, a defining facet of Mourinho's inter was his willingness and ability to deploy players to counter specific threats or bring specific abilities to a game. On the right, Mon provided more width and was a more attacking presence than his left back counterpart. For this to work, Mourinho relied on Esban Cambiaso's superb reading of the game. The Argentine midfielder could move back or across to cover, allowing Micon to push up behind Samuto, who drifted infield to support Diego Molito. Etto's role and that of Goran Pandev are rightly hailed as examples of Mourinho's ability to get players to buy into his tactical systems, even at the expense of their own normal playing style. Whileto did drift centrally to assist Milito in many games, he was also used almost as a defensive winger when required. And Panddev, nominally a striker, played a similar role on the left. This meant that in games where Mourinho needed defensive solidity, the 42-31 almost reverted to a 4411. Inter sat deep and countered, relying on the predatory instincts of Diego Molito. the awareness and creativity of Wesley Schneijder at 10 and Cambiaso's ability to pick a long pass. Inter would win the ball back, get it to Cambiaso or Schneder and would then attack from deep with long passes wide using the Dutch 10's ability to play in Molito or Etto. Dejan Stanovic, the more attacking minded central midfielder, got up to support while Schneider also dropped off to win the ball back as well as pushing forwards to assist Molito. Etto would cut inside with Mon supporting him and Panddev could do the same, although this occurred less. Indeed, Mourinho famously even used Christian Shivu, a left back in left midfield against Barcelona in the second leg of the Champions League semi-final at the New Camp to block the left hand side of the pitch. Molito, Etto, and Schneider were the team's main goal threats. Mourinho was not afraid to sacrifice attacking ability to counter the threat of Messi on Barcelona's right-hand side, just as he was not afraid to match Chelsea's 4123 with a 4-33 in the Champions League round of 16 away leg. Man marking Chelsea's system at the expense of his own attacking options. His side made no effort to hog possession either, instead relying on a clinical ability to convert the rare chances that came their way from the counter. Pragmatic, organized, tactical, yes. Defensive and boring, not always. Jose Mourinho's superb in of 200910 built by him with the additions of Schneijder, Lucio, Etto, Malito, Panddev, and M to the squad he inherited in 2008 is the best side Italian football has produced in the last 10 years and arguably since Saki's AC Milan Whiskey every night. title: How Exactly Do Liverpool Play Football?
content: When a football club wins the league, it's rare to see too much change. But Liverpool are a team in transition. After bringing in only Federico Kaza in the summer of 2024, in 2025, they've spent £420 million on eight players and overseen one of the most ambitious evolutions. On paper, they now have a squad that looks unbeatable. But what's actually changed? How exactly will this new Liverpool team play football? When Anna Slot arrived at Liverpool, he was careful to stress the differences between himself and his predecessor Jurgen Klopp. Maybe the only slight difference is that after we win the ball, I like to go forward just as Jurgen liked it. But I sometimes like it when players try to keep the ball and not play the difficult ball, he said in an early press conference. where Jurgen may be like the chaotic scenes in and around the penalty box. I think we're trying to find the balance between trying to create chaos at certain moments and trying to keep possession of the ball a bit longer in other moments. So for Slot, football is about finding a balance between chaos and control. But it's important to understand the kind of control that he wants. Slot inherited a squad with players well suited to attacking directly with speed. And he wants to retain this ability to move the ball quickly from one end of the pitch to the other. But rather than launching these attacks indiscriminately wherever they receive the ball, he wants them to be a little bit more selective about when they go and when they stay. This means if the conditions aren't right, then the players are encouraged to keep the ball deep in their half until more favorable conditions for attacking emerge. At that point, the players will trigger a tempo shift and move the ball forwards quickly. The difference is that they are now in much better control of the attacking conditions, having waited for the perfect moment to increase the chaos. This raises the chances of their attack being successful and lowers the risk that it could result in a turnover of the ball and a dangerous counterattack. It's also important to recognize the areas where Slot wants his team to control the ball. Given that Liverpool want to try and generate optimal attacking conditions before they trigger an attack, space becomes an important commodity. If they can create open spaces which are accessible, then their attacking play will become more dangerous. To do this, they want to retain the ball in deeper areas, baiting opponents forwards to open out more space around their defense. When you watch Liverpool under slot, you'll often see them moving the ball around the back line deep in their own half, waiting for space to open out and for good access to this space. Within this context, it's important to have players who can help move the ball from the back line into the spaces that their teammates are opening out higher up the pitch. When Slot first arrived at the club, he was able to use Trent Alexander Arnold and Virgil van Djk as players who could trigger these tempo shifts with their sharp progressive passing. And Muhammad Salah was the beneficiary of this more controlled direct play style. Heading into the 25-26 season though the dynamics of slots Liverpool have subtly changed. Perhaps most importantly, Trent Alexander Arnold left the club for Real Madrid. Although they brought in Jeremy Frimong to add to Connor Bradley in the right back position, both players are very different from the sort of profile that Alexander Arnold offered. A solution may have already been found though, possibly by accident with Frimong and Bradley both injured. Slot has used Dominic Abuzl at right back actually making up for some of Alexander Arnold's absence. But elsewhere, when it came to adding the more connective qualities that they lost with Alexander Arnold leaving, it arrived in the form of a more advanced player, Florian Vietz. Now, this raises an interesting question about Liverpool's tactical approach going forwards. Vitz is a supremely technical player who likes to take a lot of touches of the ball in order to create space for his teammates and help them exploit these openings. But, as we've seen, Slot wants his players to control the ball deeper in the field and generate spaces in front of the ball that can be exploited through tempo shifts. Now, this leaves Vitz two options. Either he drops deeper in the field to help his team progress from there, or he's involved higher up the field once the fast attacks are triggered. And neither of these two options really suit his skill set though, which means we might only see the best of him when Liverpool come up against teams who set up in a low block. The other dynamic shift that's occurred for Liverpool is the number nine spot. Across the summer of 2025, the club has gone from not really having a consistent striker to having two of the best options in world football in Alexander Isac and Ugo Ecatik. Of course, this is quite a nice problem to have, but it will be interesting to see how Slot navigates the issue of trying to fit them into the same team at the same time. Could one of them move out onto the left and play a wider role to accommodate the other? Could Slot try to use them both in central areas in some sort of two striker arrangement? Or will we see the two rotated in games so that Liverpool carry an incredible substitution threat from off the bench? And there are also questions to be raised about the impact that this could have on Muhammad Salah's output. But regardless, it's fair to say that as the new season gets underway, Liverpool have one of the most formidable attacking lineups in Europe. title: How Exactly Do Real Madrid Play Football?
content: Since Florentino Perez's appointment as president of Real Madrid in 2000, the club has been synonymous with the term Galacticos, the policy of bringing the best players in the world to the Santiago Bernabo. The logic behind it is that if you have the best names, then you should have the best team. But is that actually true? And with so many juggernauts in their squad, how exactly do Real Madrid play football? At the heart of the Galactico's approach, there is a tension that exists between the collective and the individual. Do you indulge your stars in the hope that their quality will win out, or do you force them into a tactical system and risk losing some of their shine? Under Carlo Angelotti, Real Madrid tended towards the first option, presenting his team with basic structures in and out of possession of the ball to give them the space to implement their own solutions to tactical problems. And the approach was successful. In his second stint at the club, Angelotti won two La Liga titles, two Champions Leagues, and one Copa del Rey. But from time to time, Angelotti's individuals would be overcome by a team using more collective ideas, sparking questions as to whether Reale should pivot to a more team focused approach. When Angelotti left to join the Brazil national team at the end of the 24-25 season, it appeared that the decision makers at Madrid certainly thought so. His replacement, Jabi Alonzo, was quick to emphasize the significance that collective ideas played in his understanding of football coaching. I'm more of a positional guy," he said in an early press conference, suggesting that he wanted to use these collective structures to break down the opposition. "I want a high press and immediate ball recoveries, but above all else, my priority is control. The more my team controls the game, the more comfortable I am." Now, this concept of collective control has been clearly evident in Alonzo's Real Madrid team with varying degrees of success so far. For instance, in the 2025 Club World Cup, Alonzo attempted to implement a modern out of possession approach, encouraging his side to press aggressively high up the pitch. But the players struggled to prevent their opponents from playing through them and eventually succumbed with ease to a PSG team that had shed their own individualistic tendencies under Lewis Enrique. Since then though, Alonzo has placed a clear emphasis on counterpressing before dropping off into a deeper block if they don't win the ball back immediately. This has been working early in the season, but Alonzo will want his team to develop a better sense of collective defending in order to maximize their chances of stopping the opposition from scoring in every phase. Since joining the club, Alonzo has tried to control games with the ball, adopting a high possession approach, which seeks to force the opposition deep into their own half before breaking them down. But there is a flexibility to the way that they look to accomplish this from game to game. We don't have a fixed system that I obsess over and refuse to change. Alonzo has pointed out we must always be dynamic and flexible and be able to adapt to different situations. So although they will look to control possession and territory, Alonzo's Real Madrid will be comfortable shifting between different structures in order to achieve it. At times, for example, they may use a back three, but in some fixtures, Alonzo might decide that a back four suits them better. But throughout it all, the goal never changes. They have to control the ball. Now, by implementing these collective ideas, it's clear that Alonzo wants to increase Madrid's chances of winning games in a sustainable manner. But this brings us back to the tension at the heart of Galactico's football. Because what happens if the system impedes the talents of the superstars who play in it? You see, there are a few areas where these sorts of questions have been raised. Most prominently, Alonzo has had to try to fit Kellian Mbappe and Venicius Jr. into the same starting 11. Even though both players tend to favor dropping out onto the left channel and driving at the goal from there. In general, the solution Alonzo has found has been to play Mbappe as an advanced forward and use Venicius as the left winger. But the problem this presents is that Mbappe still tends to drop out from his position into the wide areas. Although bringing the players into closer proximity is something that worked for Real Madrid under Anchelotti, the lack of a player in the center forward position can mean that it's harder to pin the opposition back line, which can reduce the amount of space that Madrid are actually able to exploit. Another area that poses a potential problem is the fullback position. With Trent Alexander Arnold joining from Liverpool this summer, Real Madrid have added one of the most creative players in the world into their squad. But as a fullback, Alexander Arnold is expected to balance his brilliance on the ball with his work off it. For a coach like Alonzo, with his emphasis on the collective aspect, this might mean that he rotates Alexander Arnold with a more defense focused option in games against sides who use their wingers as creative outlets. If he does, this will require him to navigate another tricky aspect of coaching a Galactico's team, management, as he looks to limit the playing time of a quality player who will expect to be starting regularly. You see, the fundamental principle of the collective approach to football is that a good coach should make a team better than the sum of its parts. For Real Madrid, who have some of the best parts out of any team in Europe, achieving this would make them comfortably one of the best teams in the world. But it will take time. And if Shabi Alonzo can't evidence the benefits of his approach quickly enough, then questions might be raised about whether Real Madrid should shift the balance back towards individual talent to really get the best out of their Galacticos. title: How Chelsea's Tactics Have Evolved
content: Since Todd Bowley and Blueco took ownership of Chelsea in 2022, their transfer strategy has consistently attracted criticism. They have signed 52 players in just over three years, and the perceived scattergun nature of their recruitment has confused lots of people, but it does seem as though their plan might be starting to pay off. Chelsea secured their first trophy of the Blue Co era with the UEFA Conference League and Club World Cup in 2025, while Enzo Moresca steered them back into the Champions League with a fourth place Premier League finish. Moresca's reward for this is the chance to do what no Chelsea manager has been able to do since Thomas Tukall and build on the work of his first season. So, how does he plan to do this? And just how exactly will Chelsea play football? When Moresca arrived at Chelsea, he inherited a team that Moritzio Pochettino had built to play intense direct football. He was brought in to change this, promising the more patient style that he'd learned as assistant to Pep Guardiola. But Moresca didn't do this straight away. Rather than making radical changes from the off, he leaned into Pochettino's more direct approach to ensure that his tenure didn't start with too much upheaval. But as time went by, he began to mold the team into his preferred style. One of the biggest changes he made was adding more control into Chelsea's approach on the ball. Although Pochettino's chaotic approach often brought goals, it did leave them open at the back. With the 2023 24 campaign being Chelsea's worst defensively in the Premier League era, Moresca managed to remedy this by introducing more of a short passing style which helped the team retain their shape when moving the ball forward. This made them better prepared to defend counterattacks which greatly improved their defensive record. However, last season also saw Chelsea struggling to score themselves. By slowing down their attacks, they gave opponents the chance to collapse into a low block more quickly. And while this did help Moresca produce the control that he wanted, it also exposed a problem. Chelsea lacked ways of breaking down low blocks. This wasn't just a tactical issue either. Many of the players that Blue Co have signed have struggled to adapt to this style. Even Cole Palmer, who's been Chelsea's creative talisman across the last few seasons, saw his form gradually tailing off as the campaign wore on. So the challenge facing Lesa and by extension the ownership is simple. They need to find different ways of breaking down lowblocks on a more consistent basis. Something which could go a long way towards closing the gap to the top of the table. And one way of achieving this could be through tweaking their tactics. When opponents played Chelsea last season, they found it relatively easy to defend against them in a man-oriented fashion. Moresca often set them up in a rigid box midfield with two defensive midfielders and two wingers sticking tightly to their positions. This made them predictable and as a consequence easier to defend against. But in recent matches, Moresca has attempted to introduce more fluidity to his team. His midfielders have scoped to drop out wide or push further forward during attacks while the wingers have been allowed to float inside. As fullbacks take their positions out wide. This does mean that if Chelsea lose the ball, they are more vulnerable to conceding dangerous counterattacks. But as it stands, Chelsea shape is far less predictable, making it difficult for opponents to track their players and subsequently harder to defend against. Of course, the tactics are nothing without the players, and it's clear that Chelsea see improving their depth as another way to improve. Take the left wing for example, where Chelsea possess three first choice options. Jamie Gittens is a touchline winger who boasts incredible physical gifts. Even against a low block, he can generate space to deliver a cross or a shot. Pedronetto, meanwhile, is more of a wide defensive midfielder, which has proven useful in big games. Against PSG, he tracked Ashrafikimei throughout the match and largely kept him quiet. Then there's Alejandro Ganache who profiles more like an inside forward. Something that should prove useful in more transitional games where Chelsea can play more directly. In short, Moresca is armed with a variety of options in nearly every position. Be it Liam Dilap and Jo Pedro up front or their wealth of options in midfield. This depth means that they're well placed to cope with gaps in the squad that will inevitably come up through injuries across the course of a long season. And finally, Chelsea have looked to find marginal gains in the form of set pieces. They've appointed highly rated setpiece coach Bernardo Quaver from Brenford and his impact has been rapid with four goals from corners in their first three games of the 2526 Premier League season. So if Chelsea can sustain this form while improving their open play tactics and integrate their new signings, this could be enough to beat teams as consistently as their title rivals. And if that does happen, the 2526 season might go down as the year that Blue Co's various and oftentimes confusing investments finally paid off. title: How Andrea Pirlo Sees Football
content: you can now get a 30-day trial to experience the athletic for free visit the link in the description below to try it now following the conclusion of the 2017 mls season andrea pirlo announced his retirement ending a playing career which lasted over 20 seasons and saw him earn all sorts of individual and team awards and after his playing days were behind him pierlo embarked upon a coaching journey which has been unusual his first step into the managerial side of the game was into the role of the under-23 manager at juventus a position he occupied for just nine days before being promoted to the manager of the first team taking over from the dismissed maurizio sarri though his time as manager of juventus lasted just one season his vision of football was made clear through his side's playing style in addition the paper he submitted to obtain his uefa pro coaching license was also released and available to the public a rare privilege which allows everyone to understand how pierlo sees the game so how is that in english plo's paper is entitled the football that i would like to it's a thesis on the way that he would like his team to set up and react during all phases of the game covering both team and individual principles designed to influence player behaviors and choices depending on the situation of the match within his work pierlo mentions how his ideas on football are heavily influenced by the barcelona sides of johan cruyff and pep guardiola in addition to louis van gaal's ix carlo ancelotti's milan and antonio conte's juventus side the last two in which he played of course first and foremost pierlo wishes his sides to play a form of total football a style he bases around two key foundations retaining possession of the ball as long as necessary before finishing off an attack and recovering the ball as quickly as possible with extreme intensity upon losing it pillow also requires his players to be dynamic when in possession capable of manufacturing space for others and occupying the correct spaces themselves when teammates have created them off-the-ball movement is crucial for controlled ball progression in his system players should have the ability to read opposition defenses and stretch them vertically and laterally by occupying defenders and creating spaces between the lines for other teammates this is where a player's position on paper is not as important as the actual positions they may appear in during a match with a heavy focus on maintaining control of the ball building play from the back is a key component too achieving this depends on the constant creation of diamond shapes around the ball carrier this means that the player in possession should have support behind them support laterally on either side and a player ahead of them who also positions themselves behind the next line of the opposition pressure upon each successful pass teammates should readjust their positioning to create a new diamond shape around the ball so reliance on fluidity dynamic space occupation and positional rotations is also key for dominating possession and progressing the ball plo does not see players as having traditional and functional positions but more so roles which they must be able to carry out based on movements and positioning of their teammates and there are various scenarios throughout the course of a match where this can be seen certain roles must always be occupied and it's not relevant what position the players technically have started in as long as the correct positions are being occupied for example this can happen when a central midfielder drops down into the back line filling in for a fullback who is then allowed to push forwards taking on the role of a winger who in turn drifts centrally to occupy that space which the midfielder has vacated this extreme focus on the concept of space is achieved through use of various principles which will influence the player's decisions so some examples of this include making sharp movements when marked by an opposition player to drag them away and create space for a teammate and then for the teammate to move into the newly created space in order to receive a pass this is a continuing process which never stops in turn allowing for players to freely move around the pitch other simple principles he wishes to implement include moving towards the ball carrier if he's being pressured offering them a simple outlet moving away from the ball carrier if they're not under pressure and allowing them more room carrying the ball into space to attract pressure and always looking to move into space after playing a pass a good example of this often occurs when a centre-back is in possession of the ball if he is not being pressured by the opposition the expectation is that he should carry the ball forward until he attracts an opposition defender and pulls them out of shape allowing for new spaces to be created and a teammate to move into the space on the contrary if the centre-back is in possession but being heavily pressed by the opposition the expectation is then for a player further up the pitch to drop down and offer an outlet to relieve the pressure further up the pitch there are three fundamental principles which should be maintained at all times regardless of playing personnel width must be maintained on each side of the pitch with a maximum of one player each side there must also be a minimum two players rotating in between the opposition's midfield and defensive lines and at least two players who are running into depth beyond the opposition backline so it's clear to see that pierlo has a vision of football which does not necessarily align with traditional philosophies as a player he always appeared to see title: How Liverpool's Front Three Became a Front Four
content: Since 2017, Liverpool have been synonymous with their front three. Sadio Mané, Roberto Firmino, and Mo Salah. Not only have these players brought huge quality, goal scoring, and creativity to Liverpool's front line, they've also kind of set the tone for the way that Liverpool play. So, the the energetic pressing, the aggressive movement forwards beyond the last line of defense. Liverpool kind of are their front three. Until recently, because with the signing of Diogo Jota, suddenly Jürgen Klopp has an alternative option. Now, what we've seen is Liverpool going to a 4-2-3-1. This is a system that Klopp did originally use when he came to Liverpool. It was a system that he was familiar with at Borussia Dortmund. Uh, but the 4-3-3 was very, very persistent. The only changes were were kind of in moments of crisis. Now, with the quality of Jota who's come in and is scoring goals, but also the quality of Firmino who is kind of undroppable, Jürgen Klopp is adapting. So, what are we going to see from Liverpool in this new formation? And what does that mean for Liverpool's now front four? There's very little point in describing how Liverpool played as a 4-3-3 because we kind of know this already. Um, there was a lot of pressing, the midfield stayed tight, the full backs pushed forwards. Obviously, now playing in a 4-2-3-1, there's very much a a different emphasis. So, we're going to look at some of the ways that Liverpool can benefit from this system first of all. The lineup is pretty much as expected. So, you've got Mané here on the left-hand side, Salah playing through the middle, Firmino just behind him in the the kind of the 10 slot, uh, and then Jota coming in off the right-hand side. The first thing that this does allow Liverpool to do is they can press higher up the pitch. Now, partly this is simply as a result of more numbers, but there are also some subtle changes. Firmino and Salah can effectively press as two playing together. So, that allows them both to push forwards onto the opposition center backs if they want to do that. Or, crucially, it also allows them to drop off a little bit and instead block up the central passing route to the defensive midfield of the opposition team. Now, a lot of teams will try and play through the center, particularly when they are wary of the fact that that Mané and Jota are both very, very good presses in wide areas. So, this flexibility that Salah and Firmino have, who are also both very capable presses, of either targeting the center backs if maybe they're a little bit weaker on the ball, or allowing them to have the ball, but but stopping up the middle line. So, what they can do is they can squish in there, or they can go further back towards those midfielders and and really prevent progression of the ball uh, from there. The other thing is that if Salah stays high, some teams, instead of using a two-man double pivot, will actually have uh, three midfielders. What that also means is that Firmino can drop off and and basically occupy whichever midfielder it is that likes to drop in and and collect the ball from the defense and try and build up from there. Liverpool still have three uh, progressive presses up front with with Salah, Mané, and Jota. And it allows Liverpool very much to kind of stop up the opposition, prevent them from playing out from the back, uh, and increase that pressure and that frenetic pressing ability that Liverpool have. So, particularly in in the early moments of games when the energy levels are high and the concentration is high, Liverpool can really camp out in their opponent's half, prevent any opportunities to clear the ball, and just build this kind of tension and pressure on the opposition, which in turn will will cause mistakes and will allow them to counter press and and then attack. From an attacking perspective, clearly the more players that you have uh, in the opposition uh, defensive third, the more you can do with it. So, Firmino is sort of occupying here the space between the lines, but also what you have with Salah is a player that can drop off himself and play between the lines. So, you have two different players, you know, Salah is is much quicker, he's much more looking to move into the space behind the last line of defense and and use his pace to get through and his finishing. Firmino will drop off, he'll link play and he'll pass, but they can interchange. And what this does is it causes problems for defenses because if Salah drops off, you know, does the center back go with him? Does the defensive midfielder drop in if Firmino's pushing up? Straight away this defender here is occupied and then Salah's got space to run into. That's before you even consider the fact that Mané is cutting inside here and Jota who who doesn't play quite as directly around the back as Mané, but more is looking to come inside on on this sort of angle, you know, this this is really posing problems for opposition defenses, particularly if they're playing a four-man defense. But it's it's the interchange between Firmino and Salah that that really creates the issues because by having these players that are flexible, that are working, you know, they're used to working with each other for for three seasons, four seasons now, they know what each other are thinking, and this allows Liverpool to create very, very intricate uh, passing displays at speed, uh, and get in behind defenses and cause them significant issues. There's one final thing about Liverpool's 4-2-3-1, which is kind of unique to them. Uh, although the system was developed by managers like in Spain as a way of pushing high, pressing the opposition in in their third with players forwards, generally speaking, the number 10 is yeah, it's kind of a luxury player. It's somebody who is there to play creative passes, but maybe isn't quite so engaged in in the the physical aspects of pressing. If they are a physically dynamic player, someone like a Mesut Özil, for example, it's very much in in the counter attacking sense rather than the pressing sense. But because Liverpool have Firmino, who is used to doing that as a nine, but can also play deeper with a slightly more creative aspect, it doesn't detract from what Liverpool are already good at, uh, and this is kind of, you know, specific to them and the personnel that they have available. So, you know, we're not looking at a system here like most 4-2-3-1s where where that central player in the hole has, you know, a creative role, but doesn't really do much else. You know, Liverpool can be aggressive consistently across that front four. Obviously, if you're playing four players up front and you're playing a four, which Liverpool will do. You know, I know people thought that them dropping a front three would almost certainly never happen, but I think it's much less likely that Liverpool would ever start playing three at the back. Clearly, that leaves only two players in central midfield. Now, there is a problem here because the balance of the team can be affected in that respect. So, if you've got uh, your front four pressing like this and and looking to to try and uh, you know, prevent progression of the ball from the center backs to the central midfield, that creates a two on two if the opposition are playing themselves a 4-2-3-1 or 3-4-3, for example. But, if that opposition is playing three in midfield, straight away you're outnumbered. Now, you could drop Firmino back, but of course what that does then is kind of uh, change the the balance of the pressing. Uh, you don't get the benefits of pressing so high. You're, you know, you're not able to to prevent ball progression to that central midfield quite so easily. So, you are sort of accepting that you're going to be outmanned there. Now, if the full backs push up, obviously, that that can help mitigate that balance, but then you're also leaving two center backs kind of on their own against a striker and and maybe players pushing up. That can create a three on two. That's not ideal as well. So, what it really does is it it requires these two players particularly, but also your wide players, Mané and Jota, to be a very, very effective first line of the press because if that press is bypassed, say, for example, that pass can occur there, all of a sudden, if that player's bursting forwards and that player's bursting forwards, you can create massive uh, numerical superiorities against Liverpool's back line. We saw that against Manchester City where when Sadio Mané missed his initial press uh, on the left-hand side of Liverpool, Wijnaldum suddenly had, you know, one player in significant space to mark. He had another player making a run behind him, and he had quite a lot of space towards the touchline to try and cover as well. That's not ideal. And so, Liverpool need to be very, very careful. Now, one of the ways they can do this is by keeping one of their full backs back, and that ensures maybe more of a back three. Uh, that still allows one of the other full backs to push up. Or, their full backs can tuck inside a little bit and create more of a kind of bowl shape here. That does bulk out the midfield, but it denies them the sort of width that they are used to having. Um, you know, where Trent Alexander-Arnold and Andy Robertson are getting into these spaces here so that they can make the cross-field passes that they do and they can open teams up with switches. So, it will require a little bit of adaptation. Both of these wide players, Mané tending to come around the outside to come in, Jota moving inside a little bit more, they are wide players who start wide and move in field. So, there is a danger here that Liverpool, because of the requirement to balance their defensive position and also the natural instinctive movements of their front line, could end up being robbed of width because these central midfielders aren't going to want to move into the wide spaces either without somebody holding in that space where we can see the opposition 10. That really though is the only weakness. You know, Liverpool are probably able to mitigate that with the the physicality and and and the speed of their players. The the fact that players like Andy Robertson and Trent Alexander-Arnold can occupy much of the flank that they work in will will try and protect those sorts of areas. If you've got people like Fabinho, Henderson, Wijnaldum in your central midfield area, you do have a lot of physicality and a lot of mobility there. So, you know, this is not necessarily going to cause Liverpool significant issues. However, as we saw against Man City, if you have four players forwards and that initial line of the press is bypassed, it can open Liverpool up and that is something that they'll have to be wary of. So, we've seen the pros and cons of Liverpool's new front four. There is of course another issue here and probably one of the things that that Jürgen Klopp is grateful for that he can use the front four at the moment is that Liverpool have got something of an injury crisis currently. So, with Van Dijk, Gomez, Fabinho, Naby Keïta, Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain, Thiago, there are a large number of players out who would certainly be contesting for if not guaranteed first team positions. If you've got four up front and you've got four in defense, you only need to fill two spaces in the middle. And Liverpool have been particularly struck in that area with injury issues. So, we've got Van Dijk and Gomez as the center backs in our lineup here, but obviously they're both currently injured. Fabinho can play there when he comes back. In midfield, while it's currently Wijnaldum and Henderson, they played against Man City, you could have Thiago in there, you could have Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain in there. This front four is solid and obviously if one of them falls to injury, let's say we'll take Firmino out there and pretend that he's injured and somebody else, that front three still looks mighty effective and then you can play a three-man midfield back to the same sort of system. So, Klopp here is dealing with two issues. One of them is a positive, the form of Diogo Jota, one of them is a negative, the injury crisis, but there's no doubt that in settling on a front four, Jürgen Klopp is currently solving both of them.

title: Catenaccio
content:
Catenaccio (Italian pronunciation: [kateˈnattʃo]) or The Chain is a tactical system in football with a strong emphasis on defence. In Italian, catenaccio means "door-bolt", which implies a highly organised and effective backline defence focused on nullifying opponents' attacks and preventing goal-scoring opportunities.


== History ==


=== Predecessors and influences ===
Italian catenaccio was influenced by the verrou (also doorbolt or chain in French) system invented by Austrian coach Karl Rappan. As coach of Switzerland in the 1930s and 1940s, Rappan played a defensive sweeper called the verrouilleur (literally "the one who locks the door"), positioned just ahead of the goalkeeper. Rappan's verrou system, proposed in 1932, when he was coach of Servette, was essentially a modification of the 2–3–5 system, and in some ways resembled the modern 4–4–2 or 4–3–3 formations; his system implemented with four defenders, three of which were fielded in a fixed role playing a strict man-to-man marking system, plus an attacking centre-half, who would also act as a playmaker, in the middle of the field, who played the ball together with two midfield wings. The system was essentially a 1–3–3–3 formation, with the verrouilleur as the last player in front of the goalkeeper, and with the two outside forwards or wingers functioning as forwards high up the pitch, keeping possession of the ball and always looking to cross the ball to the central striker making runs into the box or looking to find a pass to the most forward midfielder making a run in behind the opposing defense from the midfield. (with the right winger sitting slightly further back), but who would often drop off into deeper midfield roles when possession was lost. The team would often sit back and defend during matches, which enabled them to overcome stronger teams or physically fitter opponents successfully. In his 2009 book Inverting the Pyramid, Jonathan Wilson notes that the "verrou ... is best understood as a development from the old 2–3–5 ... . Rather than the centre-half dropping in between the two full-backs, as in the W-M, the two wing-halves fell back to flank them. They retained an attacking role, but their primary function was to combat the opposition wingers. The two full-backs then became in effect central defenders, playing initially almost alongside each other, although in practice, if the opposition attacked down their right, the left of the two would move towards the ball, with the right covering just behind, and vice versa. In theory, that always left them with a spare man–the verrouilleur as the Swiss press of the time called him or the libro as he would become–at the back." Wilson notes that a weakness of the verrou system was that it placed excessive demands on the centre-half, as the player deployed in this role was required to attack and act as a playmaker when on the ball, while instead dropping back into the defence, acting almost as a centre-back, off the ball. With this system, Rappan won two league titles with Servette, and five more with Grasshopper, after joining the club in 1935.
During his time with Soviet club Krylya Sovetov Kuybyshev in the 1940s, Alexander Kuzmich Abramov also used a similar defensive tactic known as the Volzhskaya Zashchepka, or the "Volga Clip." Unlike the verrou, his system was not as flexible, and was a development of the 3–2–5 or WM, rather than the 2–3–5, but it also featured one of the half-backs dropping deep; this allowed the defensive centre-half to sweep in behind the full-backs, essentially acting as a sweeper. In Spain, starting in the 1940s and reaching great success in the 1950s, Helenio Herrera developed an early version of his 1960s catenaccio. With Atlético Madrid (1949–1953), he won two consecutive league titles with a defence nicknamed "the Iron Curtain". He kept on developing his system later on in other Spanish clubs until reaching his well-known 5–3–2 formation when he went years later to Inter in Italy (see below).
Italian Catenaccio has its roots with Mario Villini of Triestina in the 1941 season, Ottavio Barbieri of Spezia in the campionato Alta Italia 1944, and Gipo Viani of Salernitana in the 1948 season. Mezzo sistema was influenced by Rappan's verrou and originated from an idea that one of the club's players altered the English WM system – known as the sistema in Italy – by having his centre-half-back – known as the centromediano metodista or simply metodista, in Italy – retreat into the defensive line to act as an additional defender and mark an opposing centre-forward, instead leaving his full-back (which, at the time, was similar to the modern centre-back role) free to function as what was essentially a sweeper, or libero ("free" in Italian). Although this ultra-defensive strategy was initially criticised by members of the Italian press, including journalist Gianni Brera, Andrea Schianchi of La Gazzetta dello Sport notes that this modification was designed to help smaller teams in Italy, as the man–to–man system often put players directly against one another, favouring the larger and wealthier teams with stronger individual players.
In the 1946 season, Ottavio Barbieri introduced the sweeper role to Italian football during his time as Genoa's manager. He was influenced by Rappan's verrou, and made several alterations to the English WM system or sistema, which led to his system being described as mezzosistema. Gipo Viani, after him, called this "Vianema". His system used a man-marking back-line, with three man-marking defenders and a full-back who was described as a terzino volante (or vagante, as noted at the time by former footballer and Gazzetta dello Sport journalist Renzo De Vecchi); the latter position was essentially a libero. The team's midfield played in a triangular shape, with the centre-half-back or metodista fielded in front of the back-line. His formation also made use of three forwards in attacking trident, but the right-sided winger was also tasked with assisting the midfield defensively, and therefore acted in the manner of a right-sided wide midfielder, known as the tornante in Italian football.


=== Italian catenaccio ===
In the late 1950s, Nereo Rocco's Padova pioneered a modified catenaccio tactics in Italy where it would be used again by other Italian teams throughout the 1960s; his strategy was initially also known as the mezzosistema, as, like the vianema, it modified elements of the sistema. Rocco's tactic, often referred to as the real Catenaccio, was shown first in 1947 with Triestina: the most common mode of operation was a 1–3–3–3 formation with a strictly defensive team approach, while his team would look to score by starting quick counter-attacks with long balls after winning back possession. With catenaccio, Triestina finished the Serie A tournament in a surprising second place. Some variations include 1–4–4–1 and 1–4–3–2 formations. He later had great success with Milan using the catenaccio system during the 60s and 1970s, winning several titles, including two Serie A titles, three Coppa Italia titles, two European Cups, two European Cup Winners' Cups, and an Intercontinental Cup.
Alfredo Foni used the catenaccio tactic successfully with Inter during the early 1950s; unlike Rocco, the teams's strong defensive play off the ball did not limit the offensive manner in which his team played while in possession of the ball. In his system, his team's right winger, Gino Armano, would drop back to mark the opposing team's left winger (essentially acting as a tornante), allowing Ivano Blason, the right-back, to shift across and act as a sweeper and clear balls away. Blason also played as a sweeper under Rocco; as such, he is often considered to be the first true sweeper in Italian football. The key innovation of Catenaccio was the introduction of the role of a libero defender (sweeper) who was positioned behind a line of three defenders. The sweeper's role was to recover loose balls, nullify the opponent's striker and double-mark when necessary. Another important innovation was the counter-attack, mainly based on long passes from the defence.
In Helenio Herrera's version of catenaccio in the 1960s, he used a 5–3–2 formation, in which four man-marking defenders were tightly assigned to the opposing attackers while an extra player, the sweeper, would pick up any loose ball that escaped the coverage of the defenders. The emphasis of this system in Italian football spawned the rise of many top Italian defenders who became known for their hard-tackling and ruthless defending. Despite the defensive connotations, Herrera claimed shortly before his death that the system was more attacking than people remembered, saying "the problem is that most of the people who copied me copied me wrongly. They forgot to include the attacking principles that my Catenaccio included. I had Picchi as a sweeper, yes, but I also had Facchetti, the first full back to score as many goals as a forward." Although his Grande Inter side were known primarily for their defensive strength, they were equally renowned for their ability to score goals with few touches from fast, sudden counter-attacks, due to Herrera's innovative use of attacking, overlapping full-backs. Under Herrera, Inter enjoyed a highly successful spell, which saw them win three Serie A titles, two European Cups, and two Intercontinental Cups.
Manager Ferruccio Valcareggi used tactics inspired by the Italian catenaccio system, which was popularised by Inter manager Herrera during the 1960s, with the Italy national team, employing a sweeper behind two man–marking central defenders and a full-back, as well as a strategy which made use of heavy defending, focussing predominantly on stability, grinding out results while conceding few goals and defending narrow leads; although his tactics were controversial – in particular as during the 1970 World Cup in Mexico, he devised his infamous staffetta (relay) policy of playing one of his two star playmakers, Sandro Mazzola and Gianni Rivera, in each half, to avoid offsetting the defensive balance within his team – and not particularly exciting, they proved to be effective. Moreover, although at times he drew criticism in the Italian media over Italy's dull, slow gameplay and lack of goals, Italy also demonstrated their offensive capabilities throughout the tournament, as well as their technical capabilities, which enabled them to conserve energy and cope with the altitude in Mexico. He had a successful spell as Italy's manager, winning UEFA Euro 1968 on home soil, and leading Italy to the 1970 World Cup final; however, in the latter match, Italy suffered a heavy 4–1 defeat to a much more offensive minded and stylish Brazilian side. His team adopted a more attractive playing style in the lead-up to the 1974 World Cup, which saw them considered among the favourites to win, but suffered a surprising first-round elimination in the final tournament.


=== Decline of catenaccio with the advent of total football, and the birth of zona mista ===
Jock Stein's Celtic defeated the catenaccio system in the 1967 European Cup Final with a highly offensive strategy. They beat Herrera's Inter Milan 2–1 on 25 May 1967, creating the blue print for Rinus Michels' total football, a continuation of Stein's free flowing attacking football. Total Football, which was invented by Dutch manager Rinus Michels in the 1970s, exposed the weaknesses of the Catenaccio system. Unlike previous systems, in Total Football, no out–field player is fixed in their nominal role; anyone can assume in the field the duties of an attacker, a midfielder or a defender, depending on the play. Due to players often switching positions with one another, man-marking strategies, such as catenaccio, were no longer effective at coping with this fluid system. Despite previously losing out 4–1 to Milan in the 1969 European Cup Final, who were managed by Rocco, a manager known for his defensive catenaccio strategy, in 1972, Michels' Ajax defeated Inter 2–0 in the European Cup final, and Dutch newspapers announced the "destruction of Catenaccio" at the hands of Total Football. The following year, Ajax defeated Cesare Maldini's Milan 6–0 in the second leg of the European Super Cup, in a match in which the defensive catenaccio system employed by Milan was unable to stop Ajax, which saw the Dutch side win the title 6–1 on aggregate; this was the worst defeat for an Italian team in an UEFA competition final.
As man-marking alone was insufficient to cope with the fluidity of total football, coaches consequently began to create a new tactical system that mixed man-marking with zonal defence in order to counter this strategy, which came to be known as zona mista ("mixed zone" in Italian), or gioco all'italiana ("gameplay in the Italian manner" in Italian), in Italian football, as it mixed elements of Italian catenaccio (man-marking) with elements of total football (zonal marking). Italian manager Giovanni Trapattoni, who had played under Rocco at Milan, and was initially influenced by Rocco's catenaccio system, was one of the main proponents of this system from the 1970s onwards, and used it to great success.


== Modern use of catenaccio ==


=== Derivative defensive strategies ===
Highly defensive structures with little attacking intent – which are colloquially often referred to as "anti-football" or "parking the bus", and which have been employed at times by managers such as Jose Mourinho and Diego Simeone – are often arbitrarily and incorrectly labelled as Catenaccio by pundits, managers, and players, but this deviates from the original design of the system; while catenaccio was similarly an organised system that involved tactical discipline and deep, heavy, and patient defending off – or even behind – the ball, it also made use of now obsolete man-to-man marking, a sweeper, who was tasked with protecting the back-line and also starting plays after winning back possession, as well as employing sudden counter-attacks to score goals.


=== Italian football ===
Although Catenaccio has still come to be associated with the Italy national side and Italian club teams, due to its historic association with Italian football, it is actually used quite infrequently by Serie A and Italy national teams in contemporary football, who instead currently prefer to apply balanced tactics and formations, mostly using the 5–3–2 or 3–5–2 system. For example, under manager Cesare Prandelli, the Italy national team also initially used the 3–5–2 formation, which had been popularised by Juventus manager Antonio Conte throughout the previous Serie A season following his success in the league; although Prandelli used a ball–playing sweeper, he also used attacking wing-backs and a more offensive–minded approach with Italy. In their first two clashes of UEFA Euro 2012 Group C, the system resulted in two 1–1 draws against Spain and Croatia. He subsequently switched to a stylish attacking possession-based system using their 'standard' 4–4–2 diamond formation for the knockout stages; the switch proved to be effective, as the team went on to reach the final, where they suffered defeat to a similarly more offensive-minded Spain side, who used a possession–based strategy based on passing known as tiki-taka. Rob Smyth of The Guardian was critical of Spain's striker–less formation and particular brand of tiki-taka at UEFA Euro 2012, believing that the lack of emphasis on the offensive aspect of the game led to fewer goals, and that the team's seemingly endless passing and preoccupation with ball–possession was in fact boring, dubbing it "Tiki-takanaccio", a reference to the defensive–minded catenaccio tactical system, despite the fact that tiki-taka had ironically originated from the more offensive minded Dutch total football strategy. Prandelli did make use of a more organised and defensive 3–4–3 formation against Spain during the 2013 FIFA Confederations Cup semi-final, attempting to stifle Spain's possession game by reducing spaces, and subsequently hitting them on the counter-attack; the system proved to be more effective, as Italy created several opportunities and were only eliminated on penalties following a goalless draw.
Several of Italy's previous coaches, such as Cesare Maldini and Giovanni Trapattoni, used elements of catenaccio to a greater extent at international level, and both failed to go far in the tournaments in which they took part; under Maldini, Italy lost on penalties to hosts France in the 1998 FIFA World Cup quarter-finals, following a 0–0 draw, while Trapattoni lost early in the second round of the 2002 FIFA World Cup to co-hosts South Korea on a golden goal, and subsequently suffered a first-round elimination at UEFA Euro 2004. Other Italian managers have often deviated from the catenaccio system, despite still employing aspects of the strategy into their gameplay, and maintaining a strong defensive unit. While Dino Zoff's 5–2–1–2 system initially largely differed from the more defensive-minded approach of his predecessors who were in charge of the Italy national side, by introducing younger players and adopting a more attractive and offensive-minded approach, he also made use of a sweeper, a tight back-line, and put Catenaccio to good use for Italy in the semi-final of UEFA Euro 2000 against co-hosts Netherlands, when the team went down to ten men; despite coming under criticism in the media for his defensive playing style during the match, following a penalty shoot-out victory after a 0–0 draw, he secured a place in the final. In the final, Italy only lost on the golden goal rule to France.
Previously, Azeglio Vicini, on the other hand, had led Italy to the semi-finals of both UEFA Euro 1988 and the 1990 FIFA World Cup, on home soil, thanks to a more attractive, offensive-minded possession based system, which was combined with a solid back-line and elements of the Italian zona mista ("mixed zone" in Italian) approach, or gioco all'italiana, which was a cross between zonal marking and man-marking systems, such as catenaccio. Despite their more aggressive attacking approach under Vicini during the latter tournament, Italy initially struggled in the first round, before recovering their form in the knock-out stages, and produced small wins in five hard-fought games against defensive sides, in which they scored little but risked even less, totalling only seven goals for and none against leading up to the semi-finals of the competition. Italy would then lose a tight semi-final on penalties following a 1–1 draw with Argentina, due in no small part to a more defensive strategy from Carlos Bilardo, who then went on to lose the final 1–0 to a much more offensive-minded Germany side led by manager Franz Beckenbauer. Italy then claimed the bronze medal match with a 2–1 victory over England.
Vicini's successor as the Italy national side's manager, Arrigo Sacchi, also attempted to introduce his more attacking–minded tactical philosophy, which had been highly successful with Milan, to the Italy national team; his tactics, which were inspired by Dutch total football, made use of an aggressive high-pressing system, which used a 4–4–2 formation, an attractive, fast, attacking, and possession-based playing style, and which also used innovative elements such as zonal marking and a high defensive line playing the offside trap, which largely deviated from previous systems in Italian football, despite still maintaining defensive solidity. Italy initially struggled to replicate the system successfully, and encountered mixed results. Under Sacchi, Italy reached the final of the 1994 FIFA World Cup after a slow start, only to lose on penalties following a 0–0 draw with a defensive–minded Brazilian side, but later also suffered a first-round exit at Euro 1996.
Previously, at the 1978 FIFA World Cup, Enzo Bearzot's Italian side also often adopted an attractive, offensive-minded possession game based on passing, creativity, movement, attacking flair, and technique, due to the individual skill of his players; the front three would also often change positions with one another, in order to disorient the opposing defenders. Italy finished the tournament in fourth place, a result they replicated two years later at UEFA Euro 1980 on home soil. At the 1982 FIFA World Cup, he instead adopted a more flexible and balanced tactical approach, which was based on the zona mista system, and which used a fluid 4–3–3 formation, with Gaetano Scirea as a sweeper, who held both defensive and creative duties. While the team were organised and highly effective defensively, they were also capable of getting forward and scoring from quick counter-attacks, or keeping possession when necessary. The system proved to be highly effective as Italy went on to win the title. Bearzot's Italy side were also known for their solidity, aggression, and defensive strength, possessing a number of hard–tackling players in their team, such as midfielder Marco Tardelli, and defenders Claudio Gentile and Giuseppe Bergomi. Gentile, who served as the team's stopper, or man-marking centre-back, gained a degree of infamy in the media for his highly physical man-marking of Diego Maradona in Italy's second-round match against Argentina; although controversial, the strategy proved to be effective as Gentile essentially nullified the Argentine playmaker's impact on the game, with Italy winning the match 2–1.
Similarly, although Italy successfully used a more offensive-minded approach under manager Marcello Lippi during the 2006 FIFA World Cup, which saw a record ten of the team's 23 players find the back of the net, with the side scoring 12 goals in total as they went on to claim the title, the team's organised back-line only conceded two goals, neither of which came in open play. Notwithstanding their more attacking minded playing style throughout the tournament, when Italy was reduced to ten men in the 50th minute of the 2nd round match against Australia, following Marco Materazzi's red card, coach Lippi changed the Italians' formation to a defensive orientation which caused the British newspaper The Guardian to note that "the timidity of Italy's approach had made it seem that Helenio Herrera, the high priest of Catenaccio, had taken possession of the soul of Marcello Lippi." The ten-man team was playing with a 4–3–2 scheme, just a midfielder away from the team's regular 4–4–2 system. In a tightly contested match, Italy went on to keep a clean sheet and earned a 1–0 victory through a controversial injury-time penalty. 
During his tenure with the Italy national team, Conte returned to Italy's traditional tactical roots, adopting a more organised, defensive-minded, counter-attacking approach, due to the perceived lack of talent in the side at the time, as well as injuries to key players. He used a fluid 3–5–2 formation at UEFA Euro 2016, in which the wide midfielders or wingbacks effectively functioned as wingers in a 3–3–4 formation when attacking, and as fullbacks in a 5–3–2 formation when defending behind the ball. Conte's tactics proved to be effective as Italy reached the quarter-finals, only losing out to Germany on penalties. Despite the team's defensive solidity, he refuted claims in the media that the team's style of play was based on catenaccio, in particular following Italy's offensive displays in their 2–0 victory over defending champions Spain in the round of 16. 
During Italy's victorious UEFA Euro 2020 campaign, Roberto Mancini – who once had a reputation for being a more defensive-minded and pragmatic manager – instead built on the work of Maurizio Viscidi at youth level, as well as Maurizio Sarri, Roberto De Zerbi and Gian Piero Gasperini in Serie A, using a 4–3–3 formation and an attractive, attacking style based on fluid passing in possession – built around the gameplay of the midfield trio of Marco Verratti, Jorginho and Nicolò Barella – and energetic pressing and counterpressing out of possession. En route to winning the title, Mancini's side broke the record for most goals scored by an Italian side during a major international tournament.


=== Other examples ===
Catenaccio in its purer form has had its share of success stories in recent years. German coach Otto Rehhagel used a similarly defensive approach for his Greece side in UEFA Euro 2004, with the team defending deeply behind the ball, and putting pressure on their opponents, while Traianos Dellas operated as a sweeper behind the back-line. Under Rehhagel, Greece surprisingly went on to win the tournament, despite Greece being considered as underdogs prior to the competition. Despite strong emphasis on defence, only one Greek game went into extra time, which the Greeks won with a Golden goal by Traianos Dellas. Trapattoni himself also successfully employed aspects of the system in securing a Portuguese Liga title with Benfica in 2005 – the club's first in 11 years – and had also successfully used elements of the strategy in his gioco all'italiana or zona mista tactical system with several Italian clubs throughout his career, which blended aspects of zonal marking from Dutch total football with aspects of man-marking found in Italian catenaccio.
In contrast to previous editions of the tournament, during the 2018 FIFA World Cup, several teams found success against opponents who dominated possession by adopting a more defensive style and instead maintaining a deep, disciplined, and narrow defensive line, while also looking to score on counter-attacks. In addition to recent success with intricate passing and quick counter attacks, Croatia has found success with what is termed in the media as "the bunker" (bunkerica in Croatian) style tactical approach. This approach is characterized by nearly every player behind the ball, killing the game through tactical fouling, time-wasting and playing for the result the team needs as opposed to a victory. This approach is only typically employed against very successful teams and often in away matches.
Several teams have found limited success in the 2020s employing the “park the bus” strategy against more skilled opponents, however, this strategy has generally fallen out of favour.


== Legacy ==
Although pure catenaccio is no longer as commonplace in Italian football, the stereotypical association of ruthless defensive tactics with the Serie A and the Italy national team continues to be perpetuated by foreign media, particularly with the predominantly Italian defences of AC Milan of the 1990s and Juventus from the 2010s onwards being in the spotlight. Rob Bagchi wrote in British newspaper The Guardian: "Italy has also produced defenders with a surplus of ability, composure and intelligence. For every Gentile there was an Alessandro Nesta." Critics and foreign footballers who have played in the Serie A have described Italian defenders as being "masters of the dark arts", motivated by a Machiavellian philosophy of winning a game at all costs by cunning and calculating methods. Historian John Foot summed up the mentality as "the tactics are a combination of subtlety and brutality. ... The 'tactical foul' is a way of life for Italian defenders."
